claims.text: In rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys, inherent chemical disorder creates nanoscale lattice distortions.
Nanoscale lattice distortions yield a broad distribution of local magnetic transition temperatures.
A distributed magnetic transition enables a strong magnetocaloric effect at lower applied fields.
The distributed transition keeps energy barriers low and thereby minimizes hysteresis.
The distributed transition preserves pathways for rapid heat exchange and mechanical stability.
The as-cast alloy has intrinsic chemical disorder and moderate lattice distortions.
Controlled annealing will enhance nanoscale heterogeneities and refine local lattice distortions.
Enhanced nanoscale lattice distortions and chemical heterogeneity modulate local magnetic exchange interactions.
Annealing increases variation in local exchange interactions by accentuating nanoscale structural distortions.
Increased variation in local exchange interactions broadens the distribution of local Curie temperatures.
Under a low magnetic field, a broader distribution of local Curie temperatures allows a larger fraction of local regions to contribute to magnetocaloric entropy change.
Low energy barriers minimize hysteresis losses.
Maintained lattice connectivity preserves rapid heat conduction and mechanical robustness.
Relative to the as-cast baseline, annealed samples will have a higher magnetocaloric entropy change at applied fields below 1 T.
Relative to the as-cast baseline, annealed samples will exhibit reduced magnetic hysteresis.
Relative to the as-cast baseline, annealed samples will maintain or improve heat-exchange performance.
Relative to the as-cast baseline, annealed samples will maintain or improve mechanical properties.

The proposed mechanism should apply to rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys with similar multielement compositions and disordered microstructures at approximately 300–400 K and applied fields below 1 T.
